title: SIS-Santeda Deal Puts UK B2B Supplier Risk in Focus
excerpt: Reports of a racing-data deal with an unlicensed operator raise hard questions about supplier due diligence and shareholder exposure.
paras: Reports that Sports Information Services (SIS), the racing data and content supplier, entered a commercial arrangement with Santeda, described in trade coverage as a network supplying unlicensed brands, have moved supply-chain integrity to the top of the UK compliance agenda. Entain, which holds 23.4% of SIS, said on 1 October 2026 that it takes the matter very seriously and had raised its concerns with SIS, while stressing that it is a minority shareholder and not party to SIS's customer arrangements. The reports describe a revenue-sharing contract signed in 2022 that may still have been in force this year. The facts remain contested, and none of the allegations has been tested by a regulator or a court.

The legal significance does not depend on how those facts resolve. Under the Gambling Act 2005, supplying gambling software or content to a remote operator is itself a licensable activity, and a licensed supplier is expected to meet the Gambling Commission's licence conditions and codes of practice. A supplier that feeds products into the unlicensed market therefore faces questions about its own fitness to hold an operating licence, in addition to any criminal exposure under section 33 of the Act for facilitating unlicensed provision to British consumers.

The Commission has long said that it expects licensees to know who their commercial counterparties are. Social responsibility code provision 1.1.1 and the general licence condition on cooperation and transparency apply across the whole business, and the regulator has treated weak third-party oversight as a compliance failure in its recent settlements. A licensee that cannot show it screened customers, tested their licensing status and monitored changes over time will find it hard to argue that the failure was an isolated lapse.

Shareholders face a different but related problem. The SIS cap table is reported to include several of the largest licensed British operators, among them Entain, Evoke and Betfred. Where a licensee holds a significant stake in a business that serves unlicensed operators, the Commission may ask whether the licensee exercised influence, whether it knew, and what it did once it did know. Those questions go to the integrity limb of the personal and corporate suitability tests, and they can be asked even where the shareholding is a minority.

For operators, the practical response is a proportionate review of upstream and downstream commercial relationships. Contracts with data, content and platform suppliers should contain warranties on licensing status in every market the supplier serves, audit and termination rights triggered by regulatory action or credible allegations, and an obligation to notify changes of customers. Boards should record how they considered the risk. A well-documented decision to exit a relationship quickly will carry more weight with a regulator than a later explanation that nobody had asked the question.

Suppliers have their own exposure. A business that sells into several regulated markets at once is only as secure as its weakest customer, because a regulator in one jurisdiction may treat the conduct as relevant to the licence it grants in another. Suppliers that already operate know-your-customer procedures for regulated clients should apply the same standard to every counterparty, including resellers and white-label partners, and should be ready to evidence it on request.

It is too early to say whether the Commission will open a formal investigation or whether any licensee will face enforcement. What the episode already shows is that the unlicensed market is increasingly attacked through the commercial chain that sustains it, not only through payment blocking and advertising enforcement. Operators and suppliers that treat counterparty licensing as a continuing control, rather than an onboarding check, will be better placed when that scrutiny arrives.

title: GGL Wants Criminal Reach Over Foreign Gambling Operators
excerpt: Germany's regulator wants faster rule-making and real prosecution of offshore operators as the GlüStV 2021 review gathers pace.
paras: In an interview published on 22 September 2026, Ronald Benter of the Gemeinsame Glücksspielbehörde der Länder (GGL) set out two requests for the ongoing evaluation of the Interstate Treaty on Gambling 2021 (GlüStV 2021). First, the regulator wants more freedom to adopt measures quickly, because amendments that depend on treaty text can take years even where there is broad agreement. Second, it wants public prosecutors to pursue people who offer illegal gambling to German players from outside Germany, something Mr Benter says has almost never happened.

The second request is the more significant for the industry. Unlicensed provision to German players is already a criminal offence under section 284 of the Criminal Code, and the GlüStV 2021 backs it with administrative powers including payment blocking, network blocking and action against advertising. In practice, though, enforcement has relied heavily on administrative tools directed at intermediaries because operators based offshore are difficult to reach. The GGL's proposal is aimed at the gap between the law as written and the law as applied.

Recent events show that the criminal route is not hypothetical. On 9 September 2026 prosecutors in Frankfurt searched eleven properties in the Rhine-Main region with more than one hundred officers, and one main suspect was arrested. Five people are suspected of offering online gambling without a German licence since at least July 2021 on a commercial and gang basis, with reported stakes of about €5.86 billion and assets of around €82 million secured. These are allegations only. On 17 September the GGL said it shares its findings from payment blocking, network blocking and advertising enforcement with prosecutors.

Licensed operators should read these developments as a signal about direction, not an immediate change in the law. A treaty amendment requires agreement among the sixteen Länder, and the administrative board of the GGL, chaired by Berlin's state secretary for the interior since 1 July 2026, must balance the regulator's request for flexibility against the states' interest in democratic control. The evaluation process is the likely vehicle, so the consultation phase is where industry views on proportionality, legal certainty and delegation limits can be heard.

The compliance consequences reach beyond operators that are themselves unlicensed. Affiliates, streamers, payment providers and technology suppliers that deal with unlicensed brands are the natural next step in any prosecution strategy that follows the money. Companies in those categories should check whether any counterparty serves the German market without an authorisation, and should document the steps taken to find out. Evidence of reasonable diligence will matter if a prosecutor asks about knowledge.

Cross-border enforcement also raises well-known practical questions. Mutual legal assistance, extradition and the recognition of German gambling law in the operator's home state all affect whether a prosecution can move beyond a search warrant. Operators licensed in Malta or elsewhere in the EU who market into Germany without a GGL licence should not assume that a home licence provides protection. The EU single market gives them no right to supply gambling services in a Member State that has chosen to restrict them, a position the Court of Justice has accepted for many years.

For counsel advising on the German market, the message is to keep licence conditions, advertising practices and payment flows aligned with the GlüStV 2021 and to track the treaty evaluation closely. If the Länder give the GGL more room to act and prosecutors begin to use the criminal provisions against foreign operators, the cost of non-compliance will move from fines and blocking orders towards personal liability for managers and owners.

title: Brazil: TRF-3 Suspends Stake Injunction, Backs Uniformity
excerpt: A federal appeals court halted Stake's one-day injunction, citing equal treatment of operators under Provisional Measure 1394/2026.
paras: On 9 October 2026 the president of the Federal Regional Court of the 3rd Region (TRF-3) suspended an injunction that had allowed Stake Brazil Ltda to keep offering fixed-odds betting online. A federal judge in the 9th Civil Court of São Paulo had granted the injunction a day earlier, with effect until 25 October. The suspension followed a request from the Attorney General's Office (AGU) and remains in force until final judgment in the underlying case or a further decision by the TRF-3 presidency.

The reasoning of the suspension is as important as its result. The court said that allowing one operator to keep trading while others are subject to the restrictions in Provisional Measure 1394/2026 would produce regulatory inequality and weaken uniform enforcement. It also expressed concern that similar rulings could multiply, undermining legal certainty across the sector, and it referred to consumer protection and transparency about how games operate. The decision treats the case as one about consistent national policy, not about the merits of Stake's particular business.

That framing matters for every operator weighing a court challenge in Brazil. Individual injunctions against federal measures carry a high risk of being suspended on public-interest grounds, which in Brazilian practice allows the President of the competent court to halt a ruling that threatens public order, health, security or the economy. An injunction can therefore be lost within days, as happened here, and operators that reorganise their operations in reliance on one take on a substantial and avoidable risk.

The wider constitutional dispute has not been decided. The lawfulness of Provisional Measure 1394/2026 is the subject of three pending cases before the Supreme Federal Court (STF), ADIs 8024, 8027 and 8028. Until the STF rules, or Congress converts the measure into law with or without changes, the measure's restrictions stand, and a lower-court judge's view of its validity does not alter that. Operators that want to challenge the measure should concentrate on the collective route and the arguments being made before the STF.

For operators holding authorisations from the Secretariat of Prizes and Bets (SPA), the immediate task is compliance with the measure as it currently operates, together with scenario planning. Contracts with affiliates, payment providers and platform partners should allow for changes in product scope, and customer communications should be reviewed so that any change to the offer is explained clearly. Regulators and courts have both stressed consumer transparency, and unclear messaging during a shift in the rules is an easy target for enforcement.

Operators that are not authorised should note the other implication of the decision, which is that the courts are not treating authorisation status as a technicality. A court that declines to carve out an exception for one operator is unlikely to be receptive to arguments that an unauthorised business should be allowed to continue while its dispute is heard. The SPA has already signalled a more active enforcement agenda, and the TRF-3 ruling removes one of the routes by which operators had hoped to slow it down.

The sensible reading is that Brazil's regulated market is entering a phase in which federal policy is being applied uniformly and defended by the AGU at the highest level of the federal courts. Market participants should plan on the assumption that the measure will remain in force until the STF or Congress changes it, and should treat any interim relief as fragile.

title: Nebraska Voters Decide Online Sports Betting on 3 November
excerpt: Two measures on Nebraska's ballot would authorise online sports wagering through racinos, with rules due by 1 June 2027.
paras: Nebraska voters will decide on 3 November 2026 whether to authorise online sports betting in the state. The Secretary of State certified two petitions on 21 August 2026: a constitutional amendment, the Online Sports Wagering Authorization, which needed 127,054 valid signatures and reportedly met at least 138,473, and a statutory initiative, the Online Sports Wagering Regulation, which needed 88,938 and reportedly met at least 96,918. The campaign is run by Tax Relief Nebraska and is backed by sportsbooks and casinos.

The two-measure structure is a deliberate response to the state's constitutional framework. Nebraska has treated most gambling as restricted, and the amendment is intended to remove the constitutional obstacle, while the statutory initiative supplies the operating framework. Both must pass for the programme to work as designed, so the risk of a split outcome is a real planning consideration for any business preparing an application.

As reported, the statutory framework would let in-state racinos partner with up to two online sports betting companies to offer statewide mobile wagering. That is a restrictive market-access model. It resembles the skin-based structures seen in other states, in which a licence is tied to a land-based property and third-party brands operate under it. Operators would need to win a partner relationship with a racino, not apply independently, and the commercial terms of those partnerships would become the first real competitive event.

The campaign financing already points to the likely contenders. FanDuel and DraftKings are each reported to have committed about $3.5 million, and WarHorse Casino, operated by Ho-Chunk, Inc., has said it supports the effort and has talked with FanDuel, DraftKings and BetMGM about partnerships. Other operators and their counsel should assume that conversations are already well advanced and that exclusivity terms may be on the table.

If voters approve, the Nebraska Racing and Gaming Commission would have to adopt rules by 1 June 2027. That timetable leaves a short window for consultation on matters that normally take much longer, such as licensing criteria, technical standards, responsible gambling controls, advertising limits, integrity monitoring and tax. Stakeholders that want to influence those rules should prepare comments now, and should expect public hearings in each of the state's three congressional districts, dates for which have not yet been set.

Campaign materials emphasise property tax relief, but the available reporting does not state the tax rate. That is a significant gap for operators modelling returns. Tax treatment of promotional spending, handling of free-bet credits and the allocation of revenue between racino and operator will all affect whether the market is attractive, and they may be settled in the statute or left to the Commission.

Nebraska is also a useful test of the wider political mood. Other states have recently debated tighter limits on promotions, push notifications and credit card funding, and a measure passing with a tight operating framework would show voters still back access when it comes with a fixed structure. For operators, the work to do before 3 November is to prepare partnership strategy and a compliance plan, and to be ready to act quickly if the vote is favourable.

title: EU Gambling Levy: Draft Budget Omits It, Fight Continues
excerpt: Reports say the first draft of the EU 2028 budget leaves out a common online gambling tax, but the proposal remains politically alive.
paras: Trade reports on 13 October 2026 said that the first draft of the EU budget for 2028 prepared under the Irish Council Presidency leaves out a common tax on online gambling. The draft is part of the negotiations on the 2028 to 2034 Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), which the European Commission has proposed at a minimum of €2 trillion. Reports of the text are brief and the document itself has not been seen by us, so the omission should be treated as a reported position and not a final decision.

The idea originated in the European Parliament. Romanian MEP Victor Negrescu proposed in June 2026 a levy of 1% to 2% on online gambling and betting, which he argued could raise at least €4 billion a year from 2028. Members of the Socialists and Democrats group supported a Union-level tax as both a revenue source and a first step towards harmonising fragmented gambling rules, and argued it would help licensed, tax-paying operators against unlicensed competitors.

Opposition has been firm. Malta's Prime Minister Robert Abela said he will reject any EU-wide gambling levy, arguing that taxation and fiscal sovereignty are national competences. Malta has the most to lose from a single EU tax, given the weight of MGA-licensed businesses in its economy. EU tax proposals generally require unanimity among the 27 Member States, which gives any single government a veto, and the reported omission from the Irish draft is consistent with a presidency trying to assemble a text that all capitals can accept.

Ireland's position is also shaped by its own policy. It took over the Council Presidency on 1 August 2026, and it is in the middle of reforming domestic gambling regulation through the Gambling Regulatory Authority of Ireland. It is also reported to be considering changes to betting duty at home. A presidency that is seen to favour or oppose a particular own resource risks its neutrality, so leaving the levy out of a first draft does not tell us how Ireland would vote on a later version.

For operators, the commercial concern is cumulative taxation. Most major markets already tax gross gaming revenue or turnover at national level, and several have recently raised rates. An additional EU-level charge would sit on top of national duties unless it was designed as a credit or a replacement. A levy of 1% to 2% on stakes would be far heavier than the same percentage on gross revenue, so the tax base would matter more than the headline rate, and no base has been settled.

Counsel should separate two scenarios. If the levy is dropped from the MFF package, the pressure for a common approach will not disappear, but it will probably return through other channels, such as harmonised rules on advertising, cross-border enforcement or anti-money laundering supervision under the new EU authority. If it returns in a later draft, the legal basis, the definition of taxable activity and the treatment of operators licensed in one Member State but serving customers in another will become the main negotiating points.

The sensible course for groups with EU exposure is to model the sensitivity of their margins to a possible levy, track the Council negotiating texts rather than press summaries, and engage through national associations and representatives. The reported omission is good news for the industry, but with talks continuing into 2027 it is far from conclusive.
